title: Regional road election signs ban stays in place
subtitle: Voter engagement, wording concerns in a 2021 report, and future debt and reserve fund analysis.
overview: The Administration and Finance Committee considered a staff report on the Region's election sign by-law, which has banned election signs on regional roads since 2021. A motion to direct staff to repeal the ban and return to the 2018 rules was defeated {{vote:m2}}. The ban therefore stays as it is. The committee received the report for information. Because this is a committee, any change would still need Council's adoption.

Three delegates spoke about the by-law. Supporters of the ban cited fewer removed signs, volunteer safety on busy roads, and less waste. Some councillors argued that signs are a low-cost way for new candidates to be seen. The committee also asked that wording in section D of the 2021 report be revisited in the 2025 report, saying it reflected inaccurate and stereotyping language.

The committee approved the consent agenda, which included the investment position at December 31, 2024 {{vote:m1}}. Staff also said a councillor's request about the organization's debt will be addressed in the reserve fund analysis planned for later this year.

decisions.detail: The committee defeated a motion to direct staff to draft a by-law repealing the ban on election signs on regional roads and restoring the 2018 rules {{vote:m2}}, so the current ban remains.
The committee received the consent agenda for information and approved it, including the investment position report at December 31, 2024 {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Delegates and some councillors supported keeping the ban, citing volunteer safety on busy regional roads, less plastic waste, less clutter and driver distraction, and fewer sign-related conflicts and enforcement calls.

Councillors favouring a return to signs argued they are one of the cheapest ways for new, lesser-known candidates to gain name recognition, and that the status quo helps incumbents. Some suggested limiting the number of signs.

Opponents of repeal countered that signs on private property show real support, that door-knocking is how new candidates build recognition, and that incumbents benefit from leftover signs and known locations. One councillor said signs risk becoming a de facto endorsement.

A councillor said the 2021 report's section D used stereotypes about racialized and marginalized groups and low income. Others agreed, and noted barriers to running go beyond finances. Staff said there is no precedent for amending an old report and suggested a note in the minutes.

Discussion also covered turnout and civic education: a delegate said civic education and mandatory voting merit consideration, while others pointed to existing school programs and to changing media habits among younger people.
